title: "Lists"
unit: 2

Several related values are easier to work with when they have one name. A
Python list keeps those values together and preserves their order.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* create a list
* assign a list to a variable
* find the length and sum of a list
* select a value by its position

**A list is an ordered collection of values. Each position in the list has an
index, starting at `0`.**

## Creating a list

Write a list between square brackets (`[` and `]`). Separate its values with
commas:

```{python}
[10, 20, 30]
```

The values in a list are called its **elements**. This list has three integer
elements.

A list is a value, so it can be assigned to a variable:

```{python}
marks = [10, 20, 30]
marks
```

Strings can be elements too:

```{python}
languages = ["Python", "Shell", "Markdown"]
languages
```

The order is part of the list. `"Python"` is first, `"Shell"` is second, and
`"Markdown"` is third.

## Length and sum

The `len()` function returns the number of elements in a list:

```{python}
len(languages)
```

The result is `3` because `languages` has three elements.

The `sum()` function adds the elements in a list of numbers:

```{python}
sum(marks)
```

The result is `60`, the sum of `10`, `20`, and `30`.

## Selecting an element

Use square brackets after a list name to select one element. The number inside
the brackets is the element's **index**:

```{python}
languages[0]
```

The index of the first element is `0`, not `1`. The three elements have these
indexes:

| Index | Element |
|-------|---------|
| `0` | `"Python"` |
| `1` | `"Shell"` |
| `2` | `"Markdown"` |

Use index `1` to select the second element:

```{python}
languages[1]
```

The length of `languages` is `3`, but its last index is `2`. A list with three
elements has indexes `0`, `1`, and `2`.

An index outside this range produces an `IndexError`:

```python
languages[3]
```

The last line of the error message is:

```text
IndexError: list index out of range
```

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `[10, 20, 30]` | a list with three integer elements |
| `languages = ["Python", "Shell"]` | assigns a list of strings to `languages` |
| `len(languages)` | returns the number of elements in `languages` |
| `sum([10, 20, 30])` | adds the numeric elements and returns `60` |
| `languages[0]` | selects the first element |
| `languages[1]` | selects the second element |
| `languages[2]` | selects the third element |
| `languages[3]` | raises `IndexError` when the list has only three elements |

And the one idea to carry forward: a list keeps values in order. Each value
can be selected by an index, and the first index is `0`.
